opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to what actually creates value, both for us and for the partner. In a paid engagement with no follow-through, someone hands you a problem, you build a model, you hand it back, and then it mostly disappears into a drawer. You never find out whether it worked in the real world, and you don't learn anything. For a company trying to build something genuinely new, that's a dead end.

What I care about is closing the loop. If you're doing AI for science, say designing new materials or molecules, the model is only half of it. The other half is the experiment: synthesizing the thing, testing it, seeing where your predictions were wrong, and feeding that back in. You can only do that with a partner who has real skin in the game, who has labs, domain experts, and a reason to keep iterating with you for months or years. That feedback is where the learning happens, and frankly, it's where the data comes from, which is the scarcest resource in this field.

There's also an alignment of incentives. If we share in the upside of what we discover together, both sides are motivated to push it all the way to something that matters, rather than optimizing for a deliverable on a deadline. And the trust you build lets people share problems they would never put in a short contract.

So it's not that paid work is bad. It's that deep partnerships are the only way I've seen to turn a clever model into actual impact, and impact is the whole point.

r001.rationale: The response says deep partnerships help turn a model into actual impact and that impact is the whole point, clearly expressing the opportunity to create meaningful positive change.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to what you're actually optimizing for. If somebody pays you for a one-off engagement, you deliver something, you hand it over, and then it's done. There's no feedback loop. You never learn whether the thing worked in their context, whether the assumptions you made about their data or their problem were right, and honestly that's where most of the interesting science is hiding.

With a deep partnership, you're in it together over years. Take drug discovery, or materials, or climate modeling. The people on the other side understand the domain far better than I ever will, and I understand the machine learning side. If we only talk for three months, we barely get past vocabulary. It takes a long time before a chemist and an ML researcher can actually have a productive argument. And once you get there, that's when you start asking questions neither side would have asked alone. That's genuinely where new research directions come from for me.

There's also a practical thing. Real problems are messy. The data is wrong, the objective people tell you about isn't the one they actually care about, and you only find that out after you've built something and watched it fail. A partner who's committed to the next step will tell you that. A client who paid for a deliverable will just quietly not use it.

And I'd say for the people in the lab, especially students, it's much more motivating. They see their ideas go somewhere, come back with real feedback, get iterated on. That's a very different experience from writing a report that disappears into a drawer. So for me it's less about the business model and more that deep partnerships are simply how you do good applied science.

r001.rationale: The candidate says partnerships support feedback, new research directions, and good applied science, but does not clearly state that Welling prefers them for the opportunity to create meaningful positive change.

So I’m more interested in that sustained exchange than in simply being paid for my time.
